An investment fund gets an offer of a share of a cedant's 2026 premium as a **collateralised reinsurance** deal. The insurance-linked securities (ILS) market writes this kind of deal. The fund puts collateral in a trust, and the cedant pays premium into the trust. The trust pays the losses, and the fund gets the remainder when the deal commutes.

The fund asks about the return to its investors. What return does the deal give, how likely is a loss, and how do the alternative structures compare? This document is the R twin of [`ils_deal_analysis.ipynb`](ils_deal_analysis.ipynb), with the same data, seeds and model, and its numbers agree with the notebook's numbers. It answers the questions in six steps:

1. read a submission and build the cedant's loss triangle,
2. show the historical exhibits and test how well a Bayesian model forecasts the cedant's history,
3. state an industry prior as an explicit input, and fit the cedant's ultimates against it,
4. draw the 2026 loss ratio, and apply the reinsurance structure, the collateral and the cash flows to it,
5. read the investor's IRR, MOIC and downside from the simulations, and compare two structures,
6. after binding, compare the next diagonal of actual losses with the one-year forecast.

The prose is shorter than the prose of the notebook, which explains each step. Read the two together.

**The data.** The submission is the synthetic one of `submission_evaluation.ipynb`. `examples/data/make_submission.py` wrote it from known parameters. Here the cedant offers a **20% quota share** of its commercial property book for 2026. Thus the loss to the fund is a share of the loss ratio of the cedant's whole book. All the deal terms below (the share, the commission, the collateral rule, the yield) are assumptions for the demonstration, not values in the files.

To run the document:

1. Clone the repository.
2. Install the R package (`remotes::install_github`, see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`).
3. From any folder in the repository, render with `quarto render examples/ils_deal_analysis.qmd`.

Set the environment variable `PROSPICIO_EXAMPLE_SIMS` to run fewer simulations.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)

N_SIMS <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("PROSPICIO_EXAMPLE_SIMS", "10000"))
N_ONE_YEAR <- min(N_SIMS, 1000L)  # one-year simulations for the monitoring section
SAMPLER <- list(chains = 4, tune = 600, draws = 600)  # small on purpose: the demo runs in a few minutes
SEED <- 20261023

# The submission's folder, from wherever the document renders inside the repository.
find_data <- function(start = getwd()) {
  dir <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/")
  repeat {
    for (sub in c("examples/data/submission", "data/submission")) {
      candidate <- file.path(dir, sub)
      if (dir.exists(candidate)) return(candidate)
    }
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/submission not found above ", start)
    dir <- parent
  }
}
DATA <- find_data()
read_csv <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(DATA, name), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

when <- function(text) {
  p <- as.integer(strsplit(text, "-")[[1]])
  year_fraction(p[1], p[2], p[3])
}
money <- function(x) sprintf("%.1fm", x / 1e6)

# The i-th point of a low-discrepancy sequence on (0, 1): the same numbers as the notebook, with no generator to differ.
uniform <- function(i) (0.5 + i * 0.6180339887498949) %% 1
normal <- function(i) qnorm(uniform(i))
sd_pop <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))

cat("submission files in", basename(dirname(DATA)), "/", basename(DATA), ";", N_SIMS, "simulations, seed", SEED, "\n")
```

## 1. The submission and the cedant's triangle

The files give the loss triangle (paid and incurred by accident year and age), the premium by year and the rate changes. The rate changes restate the premium of each year at the **current rate level** (the *on-level* premium). The 2026 loss ratio forecast is on the 2026 on-level premium.

```{r}
#| label: data
program_table <- read_csv("treaty_program.csv")
program <- setNames(program_table$value, program_table$item)
subject <- read_csv("subject_premium.csv")
YEARS <- subject$calendar_year
SUBJECT_PREMIUM <- setNames(subject$subject_premium, YEARS)
P_2026 <- as.numeric(program[["estimated_subject_premium_income"]])

rate_rows <- read_csv("rate_changes.csv")
effective <- vapply(rate_rows$effective_date, when, numeric(1))
onlevel <- setNames(vapply(YEARS, function(y) {
  SUBJECT_PREMIUM[[as.character(y)]] *
    rate_level(effective, rate_rows$average_rate_change, start = y, end = y + 1, term = 1)$on_level_factor
}, numeric(1)), YEARS)

tri_rows <- read_csv("triangle.csv")
tri_rows$onlevel <- onlevel[as.character(tri_rows$accident_year)]
triangle_all <- triangle(tri_rows, "accident_year", "development_months", c("paid", "incurred", "onlevel"))
cat(sprintf("cedant %s; %s; treaty year %s to %s\n", program[["cedant"]], program[["line_of_business"]],
            program[["period_start"]], program[["period_end"]]))
cat(sprintf("estimated 2026 subject premium %s; triangle origins %s to %s, %d ages\n", money(P_2026),
            triangle_all@origins[1], tail(triangle_all@origins, 1), length(triangle_all@development)))
```

## 2. Historical exhibits and a backtest

The **paid chain ladder** gives the cedant's payment pattern, which the cash-flow step needs. The **loss ratio by accident year** at its latest age, on on-level premium, shows the level and the spread to compare with the prior.

```{r}
#| label: exhibits
chain <- chain_ladder(triangle_all, "paid")
CDF <- as.numeric(chain@cdf)
AGES <- 12 * seq_along(CDF)
last_rows <- tri_rows[!duplicated(tri_rows$accident_year, fromLast = TRUE), ]
latest_incurred <- setNames(last_rows$incurred, last_rows$accident_year)
loss_ratio_now <- latest_incurred[as.character(YEARS)] / onlevel[as.character(YEARS)]

cat("paid chain ladder: age (months), factor to ultimate, share paid\n")
print(data.frame(age = AGES, cdf = round(CDF, 3), paid = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 / CDF)), row.names = FALSE)
print(data.frame(year = YEARS, on_level_premium = money(onlevel), incurred_now = money(latest_incurred),
                 incurred_lr = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * loss_ratio_now)), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: exhibit-chart
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
plot(c(0, AGES / 12), c(0, 1 / CDF), type = "b", xlab = "years since the start of the accident year",
     ylab = "share of ultimate paid", main = "Paid pattern (chain ladder)")
barplot(loss_ratio_now, names.arg = YEARS, las = 2, ylab = "incurred loss ratio at latest age",
        main = "Loss ratio by accident year")
par(op)
```

A **diagonal backtest** holds out the latest calendar diagonals. For each diagonal, it fits the model on the data known before that diagonal and scores the forecast of the cells that came next. Here the model is the Bayesian over-dispersed Poisson chain ladder on two diagonals, with a small sampler to keep the document fast.

```{r}
#| label: backtest
backtest <- diagonal_backtest(triangle_all, "paid", list(bayes_odp = do.call(bayes_odp_spec, SAMPLER)), 2,
                              n_sims = 500, seed = SEED)
cat("held-out diagonals:", paste(backtest@diagonals, collapse = ", "), "\n")
print(backtest@mean, row.names = FALSE)
if (nrow(backtest@warnings)) print(backtest@warnings)
```

## 3. The industry prior as an explicit input

The analyst writes a prior for the ultimate loss ratio, with a stated strength, as a **prior mean `m` and coefficient of variation `cv`**. `prospicio` estimates them from several programs with `hierarchical_credibility()` (Buhlmann-Straub with a normal prior on the collective mean).

The peer programs below are **synthetic** (#599, #604). A fixed low-discrepancy sequence draws them, so that this document has the numbers of the notebook. There are twelve programs with eight years of loss ratios and premium weights. The method is real. The collective mean and the distribution of the expected loss ratio of a program give `m` and `cv`. The prior on the collective mean (`collective_mean = c(0.50, 0.10)`) is the analyst's judgment about the line.

```{r}
#| label: prior
N_PEERS <- 12
N_PEER_YEARS <- 8
peer_mean <- 0.48 + 0.06 * normal(0:(N_PEERS - 1))
peer_weight <- t(sapply(0:(N_PEERS - 1), function(i) 0.5 + 1.5 * uniform(100 + i * N_PEER_YEARS + 0:(N_PEER_YEARS - 1))))
peer_ratio <- t(sapply(0:(N_PEERS - 1), function(i) {
  j <- 0:(N_PEER_YEARS - 1)
  peer_mean[i + 1] + 0.08 / sqrt(peer_weight[i + 1, j + 1]) * normal(1000 + i * N_PEER_YEARS + j)
}))

industry <- do.call(hierarchical_credibility,
                    c(list(peer_ratio, peer_weight, collective_mean = c(0.50, 0.10), seed = SEED), SAMPLER))
# The risk premiums of all groups pooled: the distribution of a program's expected loss ratio in this market.
pooled <- as.numeric(draw_matrix(credibility_predictive(industry, n_sims = 2000, seed = SEED)))
M_PRIOR <- mean(pooled)
CV_PRIOR <- sd_pop(pooled) / M_PRIOR
cat(sprintf("collective mean %.3f; a program's expected loss ratio: mean %.3f, sd %.3f, cv %.3f\n",
            industry$collective_mean, M_PRIOR, sd_pop(pooled), CV_PRIOR))
cat(sprintf("inputs used below: m = %.3f, cv = %.3f\n", M_PRIOR, CV_PRIOR))
```

## 4. The cedant's ultimates against that prior

`bayes_bf_normalised()` is the Bayesian Bornhuetter-Ferguson with the prior on the **expected ultimate** of each accident year. `apriori` is the expected ultimate loss ratio, and `cv` sets how firmly the model holds it. The model fits the **paid** triangle on on-level premium, so that its pattern is the payment pattern that the cash flows need.

The model has no tail beyond the last age. The chunk drops the oldest age for three reasons:

* only 2016 has it,
* the chain ladder shows no development there,
* the model needs the increments of every column to sum to more than zero.

```{r}
#| label: fit
fit_rows <- tri_rows[tri_rows$development_months <= 108, ]
build <- function(rows) triangle(rows, "accident_year", "development_months", c("paid", "onlevel"))
newest <- !duplicated(fit_rows$accident_year, fromLast = TRUE)
latest_fit <- setNames(fit_rows$paid[newest], fit_rows$accident_year[newest])
fit <- do.call(bayes_bf_normalised,
               c(list(build(fit_rows), "paid", "onlevel", apriori = M_PRIOR, cv = CV_PRIOR, n_sims = N_SIMS,
                      seed = SEED), SAMPLER))

origins <- as.integer(fit@origins)
exposure <- setNames(fit@exposure, origins)
ultimate_lr <- lapply(setNames(origins, origins), function(o) {  # latest paid plus the reserve draws, over premium
  (latest_fit[[as.character(o)]] + marginal(fit@reserves, as.character(o))@draws) / exposure[[as.character(o)]]
})
post_mean <- vapply(ultimate_lr, mean, numeric(1))
post_cv <- vapply(ultimate_lr, sd_pop, numeric(1)) / post_mean

cat("ultimate loss ratio, paid basis: posterior mean, cv, and the prior mean\n")
print(data.frame(year = origins, posterior = sprintf("%.3f", post_mean), cv = sprintf("%.3f", post_cv),
                 prior = sprintf("%.3f", M_PRIOR)), row.names = FALSE)
cat("pattern (share paid at each age):", paste(sprintf("%.3f", fit@pattern), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("sampler diagnostics: max R-hat", format(fit@diagnostics$max_rhat), "\n")
```

## 5. The 2026 loss ratio

The model forecasts the cells of the years in the triangle. Section 4 turns its reserve draws into a loss ratio for each simulation (#602). For 2026, a new accident year, the chunk below uses a **lognormal** (#598).

The mean of the lognormal is the average of the posterior mean ultimate loss ratios of the last five years. Loss ratios increase over the ten years and the model has no trend, so older years would understate 2026. The coefficient of variation combines three parts:

* the spread of the means of those five years,
* the average posterior cv of one year,
* the cv of the industry prior, as the uncertainty about the level in 2026.

The lognormal is a substitute for a predictive distribution.

```{r}
#| label: loss-ratio
RECENT <- as.character(tail(origins, 5))
MU_2026 <- mean(post_mean[RECENT])
CV_BETWEEN <- sd_pop(post_mean[RECENT]) / MU_2026
CV_WITHIN <- sqrt(mean(post_cv[RECENT]^2))
CV_LEVEL <- CV_PRIOR
CV_2026 <- sqrt(CV_BETWEEN^2 + CV_WITHIN^2 + CV_LEVEL^2)
sigma <- sqrt(log(1 + CV_2026^2))
mu <- log(MU_2026) - sigma^2 / 2
LR <- exp(mu + sigma * normal(10000 + 0:(N_SIMS - 1)))  # the 2026 ultimate loss ratio, one per simulation
cat(sprintf("2026 loss ratio: mean %.3f (target %.3f), cv %.3f (between years %.3f, within a year %.3f, level %.3f)\n",
            mean(LR), MU_2026, sd_pop(LR) / mean(LR), CV_BETWEEN, CV_WITHIN, CV_LEVEL))
cat("percentiles 5, 50, 95:", paste(sprintf("%.3f", sort(LR)[floor(N_SIMS * c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) + 1]), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## 6. The structure

The fund takes 20% of the cedant's subject premium and of its losses: a **quota share**. The document compares two commission terms:

* **A, flat**: a 32% ceding commission in all outcomes.
* **B, sliding scale**: the commission decreases as the loss ratio increases. It goes from 36% at a loss ratio of 45% to 24% at 70%, through 32% at 52%.

`apply_tower()` applies the contract to the 2026 annual losses (the loss ratio times the premium), one for each simulation. `deal_ratios()` gives the loss ratio, the commission, the brokerage and the margin of each simulation.

```{r}
#| label: structure
CESSION <- 0.20
BROKERAGE <- 0.025
CEDED_PREMIUM <- CESSION * P_2026
annual_loss <- LR * P_2026  # the cedant's whole-book loss, one per simulation

flat <- quota_share("A_flat", CESSION)
flat <- with_brokerage(with_ceding_commission(with_premium_rate(flat, 1, P_2026), 0.32), BROKERAGE)
sliding <- quota_share("B_sliding", CESSION)
sliding <- with_brokerage(with_sliding_scale(with_premium_rate(sliding, 1, P_2026),
                                             c(0.36, 0.32, 0.24), c(0.45, 0.52, 0.70)), BROKERAGE)

deals <- list()
for (name in c("A_flat", "B_sliding")) {
  tower <- reinsurance_tower(list(if (name == "A_flat") flat else sliding))
  result <- apply_tower(tower, annual_loss)
  ratios <- deal_ratios(tower, result, name)
  column <- function(n) marginal(ratios, n)@draws
  deals[[name]] <- list(tower = tower, result = result, loss = column("loss_ratio"),
                        commission = column("ceding_commission") + column("brokerage"), margin = column("margin"))
}
print(data.frame(structure = names(deals),
                 mean_LR = sprintf("%.3f", vapply(deals, function(d) mean(d$loss), 0)),
                 mean_comm_brkg = sprintf("%.3f", vapply(deals, function(d) mean(d$commission), 0)),
                 mean_margin = sprintf("%+.3f", vapply(deals, function(d) mean(d$margin), 0)),
                 sd_margin = sprintf("%.3f", vapply(deals, function(d) sd_pop(d$margin), 0))), row.names = FALSE)
cat("ceded premium", money(CEDED_PREMIUM), "\n")
```

## 7. Collateral and cash flows

The money moves monthly. The parts:

* **Payment pattern.** The factors of the paid chain ladder give the share of the ultimate loss paid by each age. `cashflow_terms()` takes cumulative *monthly* shares, so the chunk below interpolates the annual pattern linearly to months (#601). All simulations use the same pattern on purpose: the loss ratios `LR` are lognormal draws around the fit, and they are not paired row by row with its simulations. When the losses come from the same fit, `monthly_pattern_draws()` gives a monthly pattern for each simulation, and `cashflow_run(paid_patterns =)` pays each simulation on its own (#673).
* **Premium.** The cedant writes premium evenly over 2026 and collects it as written. The premium earns over the following two years.
* **Collateral.** The trust must hold 30% of the unearned premium plus 125% of the outstanding loss (the ultimate loss of the deal less paid to date).
* **Yield, expenses and commutation.** The trust earns 3% a year, and expenses are 0.5% a year of the requirement. At month 60 the deal commutes.

The cash-flow engine takes the ultimate loss ratio of the **deal** in each simulation and returns the investor's flows. The premium into the trust is `collected_rate` times the premium, a fixed value in the terms. The sliding scale makes the commission different in each simulation. Thus the chunk groups the simulations by commission rate, to 0.1 percentage point. It runs the engine once for each group with the `collected_rate` of that group, and puts the flows back in simulation order.

```{r}
#| label: cashflows
T_MONTHS <- 60
pattern <- payment_pattern_from_development(AGES / 12, c(pmax(1, CDF[-length(CDF)]), 1))
cum_paid <- cumsum(pattern$shares)

paid_share <- function(month) {
  # Cumulative share of the ultimate paid by the end of `month`: the annual pattern, interpolated linearly.
  t <- month / 12
  lo <- floor(t)
  a <- if (lo > 0) cum_paid[lo] else 0
  b <- cum_paid[lo + 1]
  a + (b - a) * (t - lo)
}
earned_share <- function(month) {
  t <- month / 12
  if (t <= 1) t * t / 2 else min(1, 1 - (2 - t)^2 / 2)
}
written <- pmin(1, seq_len(T_MONTHS) / 12)
earned <- vapply(seq_len(T_MONTHS), earned_share, 0)
paid <- vapply(seq_len(T_MONTHS), paid_share, 0)
duration <- sum(pattern$times * pattern$shares)
cat(sprintf("payment pattern: mean time to payment %.2f years; paid by month 12, 24, 60: %.1f%%, %.1f%%, %.1f%%\n",
            duration, 100 * paid[12], 100 * paid[24], 100 * paid[60]))

requirement <- cashflow_requirement(c("unearned-premium" = 0.30, outstanding = 1.25))
make_terms <- function(commission) {
  cashflow_terms(CEDED_PREMIUM, T_MONTHS, written, earned, paid, requirement,
                 commutation_requirement = cashflow_requirement(c(outstanding = 1.0)),
                 collected_rate = 1 - commission, annual_yield = 0.03, expense_rate = 0.005)
}

run_structure <- function(u, commission) {
  # One engine run for each distinct commission rate, flows back in simulation order.
  groups <- split(seq_along(u), round(commission, 3))
  flows <- matrix(0, length(u), T_MONTHS)
  funded <- numeric(length(u))
  opening <- numeric(length(u))
  for (g in names(groups)) {
    index <- groups[[g]]
    out <- cashflow_run(make_terms(as.numeric(g)), u[index])
    flows[index, ] <- out$flows
    funded[index] <- out$funded
    opening[index] <- out$opening
  }
  list(flows = flows, funded = funded, opening = opening)
}

for (name in names(deals)) {
  d <- deals[[name]]
  run <- run_structure(d$loss, d$commission)
  d$flows <- run$flows
  d$funded <- run$funded
  d$opening <- run$opening
  d$run <- deal_run_from_tower(name, d$tower, d$result, name, flows = run$flows, funded = run$funded,
                               opening = run$opening, patterns = list(written, earned, paid))
  # A book of one deal: its IRR and MOIC in each simulation. The IRR search starts at -95% to +100% a year.
  # The best years of this deal are above 100%, so with extend = TRUE a simulation with no root there is searched
  # above and below that range, and the root nearer 0 is taken (#675).
  book_cf <- book_cashflows(deal_book(list(d$run)), extend = TRUE)
  d$rate <- book_cf$irr$rate
  d$moic <- book_cf$moic
  deals[[name]] <- d
}
cat(length(deals), "structures run,", N_SIMS, "simulations each,", T_MONTHS, "months\n")
cat("capital called from the fund over the term, summed (mean; it is recycled as losses are paid):",
    paste(names(deals), money(vapply(deals, function(d) mean(d$funded), 0)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## 8. What the investor gets

For each structure, the chunk computes the return of each simulation:

* the **IRR**. The search starts between -95% and 100% a year. The best years of this deal are above 100%, so the chunk sets `extend = TRUE` (#675): when the search finds no root in that range, it looks above and below it, so no simulation drops out of the percentiles (#670). The chunk still excludes and counts any simulation with no root at all.
* the **MOIC**: one plus the net flows divided by the capital called from the fund.
* the downside: the probability of a negative IRR or a MOIC below 1, and the mean of the worst 5% of IRRs.

```{r}
#| label: investor
rows <- lapply(names(deals), function(name) {
  d <- deals[[name]]
  rate <- d$rate[is.finite(d$rate)]
  ordered <- sort(rate)
  pct <- function(p) ordered[min(length(ordered), floor(p * length(ordered)) + 1)]
  worst <- ordered[seq_len(max(1, length(ordered) %/% 20))]
  data.frame(structure = name, mean_MOIC = sprintf("%.3f", mean(d$moic)), IRR_p5 = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * pct(0.05)),
             IRR_p50 = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * pct(0.5)), IRR_p95 = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * pct(0.95)),
             P_IRR_neg = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(rate < 0)), P_MOIC_lt_1 = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(d$moic < 1)),
             IRR_TVaR5 = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * mean(worst)), no_root = length(d$rate) - length(rate))
})
print(do.call(rbind, rows), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: investor-chart
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
colours <- c(rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5), rgb(0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.5))
hist(deals$A_flat$rate[is.finite(deals$A_flat$rate)], breaks = seq(-0.95, 5, by = 0.025), col = colours[1],
     xlim = c(-0.5, 1.0), main = "Investor IRR", xlab = "IRR (annual)")
hist(deals$B_sliding$rate[is.finite(deals$B_sliding$rate)], breaks = seq(-0.95, 5, by = 0.025), col = colours[2],
     add = TRUE)
hist(deals$A_flat$moic, breaks = 60, col = colours[1], xlim = c(0.5, 1.6), main = "Investor MOIC", xlab = "MOIC")
hist(deals$B_sliding$moic, breaks = 60, col = colours[2], add = TRUE)
legend("topright", legend = names(deals), fill = colours, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

`risk_ratios()` takes the margin of each simulation, where large is good. It returns Sharpe, Sortino, Omega and the TVaR ratio about a threshold (here a target margin of 10%). The quantity is the deal's **margin** (one less the combined ratio), not the fund's return.

```{r}
#| label: risk-ratios
for (name in names(deals)) {
  cat(name, "\n")
  print(round(unlist(risk_ratios(deals[[name]]$margin, threshold = 0.10, tvar_levels = 95)), 3))
}
```

## 9. Comparing the structures

`book_summary()` shows the premium, loss and deductions of the structures side by side. A `deal_book()` adds its deals on the same simulated years, so its **total** row would be a portfolio that holds both structures. Read only the rows of each structure.

```{r}
#| label: compare
summary_book <- book_summary(deal_book(lapply(deals, function(d) d$run)))
summary_book <- summary_book[summary_book$deal != "total", ]
print(data.frame(deal = summary_book$deal, item = summary_book$item, mean = money(summary_book$mean),
                 ratio_to_premium = sprintf("%.3f", summary_book$ratio)), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 10. Monitoring after binding

Each quarter brings a new diagonal of actual paid losses. The check holds out the latest diagonal and fits the model on the data known one year earlier. It takes the **one-year view** (the distribution of the claims development result over the next year) and compares it with the actual diagonal.

The realised result is the opening reserve, less the amount paid in the year, less the closing reserve, for each accident year in the triangle. The model fitted to the full triangle estimates the closing reserve.

This check is on the cedant's *history* (#603).

```{r}
#| label: monitoring
valuation_year <- function(rows) rows$accident_year + rows$development_months %/% 12 - 1
last <- max(valuation_year(fit_rows))
opening_rows <- fit_rows[valuation_year(fit_rows) < last, ]
newest_open <- !duplicated(opening_rows$accident_year, fromLast = TRUE)
paid_open <- setNames(opening_rows$paid[newest_open], opening_rows$accident_year[newest_open])

view <- do.call(bayes_bf_normalised_one_year,
                c(list(build(opening_rows), "paid", "onlevel", apriori = M_PRIOR, cv = CV_PRIOR, n_sims = N_ONE_YEAR,
                       seed = SEED, one_year_sims = N_ONE_YEAR), SAMPLER))
cdr <- total(view@cdr)@draws

opening_reserve <- view@opening_reserve
closing_reserve <- vapply(names(opening_reserve), function(o) mean(marginal(fit@reserves, o)@draws), 0)
paid_in_year <- latest_fit[names(opening_reserve)] - paid_open[names(opening_reserve)]
realised <- sum(opening_reserve - paid_in_year - closing_reserve)
percentile <- mean(cdr <= realised)
cat(sprintf("valuation %d: one-year claims development result, forecast mean %s, sd %s; realised %s, at the %.0f%% percentile of the forecast\n",
            last, money(mean(cdr)), money(sd_pop(cdr)), money(realised), 100 * percentile))
```

## 11. A summary for the investor

One table of the results, as a plain printout of the quantities above (#605).

```{r}
#| label: report
report <- data.frame(item = c("2026 loss ratio, mean (cv)", "industry prior m (cv)", "ceded premium",
                              "payment pattern, mean time to payment", "backtest sampler warnings",
                              "monitoring: realised CDR percentile"),
                     value = c(sprintf("%.1f%% (%.0f%%)", 100 * mean(LR), 100 * sd_pop(LR) / mean(LR)),
                               sprintf("%.1f%% (%.0f%%)", 100 * M_PRIOR, 100 * CV_PRIOR), money(CEDED_PREMIUM),
                               sprintf("%.2f years", duration), as.character(nrow(backtest@warnings)),
                               sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * percentile)))
for (name in names(deals)) {
  d <- deals[[name]]
  rate <- d$rate[is.finite(d$rate)]
  report <- rbind(report,
                  data.frame(item = paste0(name, ": median IRR / mean MOIC"),
                             value = sprintf("%+.1f%% / %.3f", 100 * sort(rate)[length(rate) %/% 2 + 1], mean(d$moic))),
                  data.frame(item = paste0(name, ": P(IRR < 0)"), value = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(rate < 0))))
}
print(report, row.names = FALSE)
```
